01 — Why it matters

Axial parts are where a mixed-technology line quietly loses hours

Resistors, diodes, small inductors and braided jump wires still ship on paper tape — packaging that protects long leads but defeats reel-to-reel feeding. Without a dedicated axial feeder, an operator hand-picks them one by one: slow, inconsistent, and the single most common source of wrong-part and reversed-polarity escapes on high-mix boards. The SAF1001 turns that bench into a machine step that runs at the inserter's cycle.

01

Hand-picking is the hidden bottleneck

Every axial component placed by hand costs seconds the inserter could spend placing. Multiply by boards per shift and the 'small' parts decide your real output — and nobody logs it because the inserter was never the constraint.

02

Manual feeding escapes errors

A person loading axial parts from a tape reel can invert polarity, mix adjacent values, or fatigue by hour six. The SAF1001 presents one part at a time at a known pitch and attitude — the head either takes the right part or the machine alarms.

03

Changeovers burn uptime

Without a dedicated tape path, every extra part number means another reel, another stop, another qualification. Three standard tape widths (35 / 64 / 92 mm) and a customisable tray let one SAF1001 carry the axial family so lanes are swapped, not the line stopped.

02 — The method

From paper tape to insertion point in six repeatable moves

Axial tape feeding is older than SMT, but the engineering is in the details: how the tape is held, how the part is positioned, and how the U-shape is presented when the head arrives. The SAF1001 sequences it into six steps, all documented in the horizontal taped-feeder manual.

01

Load the tray

The taped reel drops into the horizontal taping tray; incoming materials arrive in boxes. The tape path runs flat, the leader is fed past the optical fibre head, and the waste-tape outlet at the front is cleared for the paper strip to drop vertically.

02

Lock onto the machine

Installation is a positioning key plus a press block — the manual's own words. Seat the feeder against the machine datum, close the locking clamp, and the feeder is defined in space. No shims, no re-tramming.

03

Sense and fine-tune

Optical fibre sensing reads the tape index; an air cylinder fine-tunes the position. Together they close the loop on feeding accuracy: ±0.3 mm at the pick, cycle after cycle. The fibre head is cleaned weekly with alcohol so dust never shifts the datum.

04

Advance the tape

The feed cylinder pushes, the cut cylinder trims the lead, and the air-pressure speed regulation sets the pace. 0.8 seconds per feed is the published figure — fast enough to keep up with the inserter, slow enough to keep the part in attitude.

05

The head picks

The insertion head descends into the pick area and takes the leading component. Because the tape is defined at three points and the part is presented at a known pitch, the pick height and offset stay the same on cycle one and cycle fifty thousand.

06

Recycle the waste tape

As parts are consumed, the paper strip advances and drops vertically out the front-end waste-tape outlet. A reflow-type take-up is optional for lines that want the strip coiled, not dropped.

Step sequence and fixturing details are quoted from the horizontal taped-feeder operation manual (卧式编带飞达使用说明书, design version 20211210A02).

Built around the service manual — maintainability as a design goal

Positioning key + press block

The manual's own fixing method: a mechanical key defines the datum, a press block clamps it. Supports custom structures when your machine wants a different footprint.

Optical fibre + air-cylinder positioning

The fibre reads the tape index; the cylinder nudges the position. Two sensors and one actuator close the accuracy circuit without a camera, without a licence fee, and without a software stack to maintain.

Feed and cut cylinders, both speed-adjustable

The internal-structure page of the manual shows the feed cylinder and the cut cylinder with independent speed adjustment. Tune the advance to the tape, tune the cut to the lead — two dials, one stable process.

Lifting-height adjustment

The manual documents a lifting-height adjust screw that sets how far the part rises into the pick zone. One setting per component family; logged on the changeover card.

Front-end vertical waste-tape drop

The paper strip falls out the front, not back into the tray. A reflow-type take-up is optional for lines that want the strip coiled for inspection or recycling.

8-core aviation plug, IO or standalone

The same connector carries 24 V, 0 V and the IO handshake (start, request, ready, clamped). Run the feeder under machine control or standalone — the manual documents both modes.

Two cylinders, one fibre and a plug — controls an operator actually uses

Manual / auto switch

The panel carries a manual-auto selector, a start key, a stop key and a reset key. In manual, the cut-key and feed-key drive the two cylinders one step at a time for setup and jam clearing.

Delay settings

The manual defines four delay parameters: material-arrival delay, feed-cylinder retract delay, cut-cylinder extend delay and cut-cylinder retract delay. Four numbers, one timing diagram.

Optical fibre amplifier

The fibre head reads the tape index; the amplifier output tells the PLC whether the part is present. The manual's troubleshooting chapter names both failure modes — always-on (broken fibre) and dark screen (broken amplifier).

IO handshake with the inserter

The manual publishes the wiring: start signal X6 from the host, ready signal Y3 back, clamped signal X7 to release the cut knife. All signals are 0 V active, switch-type, pulse-based.

06 — Installation

Six moves from crate to first part

The operation manual defines the whole commissioning: mechanical install, tape threading, IO handshake, and the four-delay tune. Plan for minutes, not hours — and have the taped reels on hand for the tuning run.

STEP 1 · Unbox and inspect

Check the body, feed cylinder, cut cylinder, optical fibre head and 8-core aviation plug against the manual's parts list. Confirm the tape path is clean and the waste-tape outlet is clear.

STEP 2 · Seat on the machine datum

Align the positioning key to the machine slot and close the press-block clamp. The manual is explicit: the feeder must be locked firmly — a loose mount is the most common cause of pitch drift.

STEP 3 · Connect air and power

0.4 – 0.6 MPa dry clean air to the inlet; 24 V DC to the aviation plug. The manual warns: never short 24 V to 0 V, and never run the inlet below 0.6 MPa or parts will not advance fully.

STEP 4 · Thread the tape

Drop the taped reel into the horizontal tray, feed the leader past the optical fibre head, and let the paper strip fall into the front-end waste-tape outlet. Leave about 100 mm of leader at the tape front so the drop arc is clean.

STEP 5 · Wire the IO handshake

The manual publishes the wiring: 24 V and 0 V to the host supply, start signal X6 from the host, ready signal Y3 back, clamped signal X7 to release the cut knife. All signals are 0 V active, switch type. Standalone mode is also supported.

STEP 6 · Tune the four delays

Set material-arrival delay, feed-cylinder retract delay, cut-cylinder extend delay and cut-cylinder retract delay until the tape advances cleanly and the lead is trimmed square. Log the four numbers per part number — your next changeover starts from a known setting.

ARTICLE 01Axial components are where a mixed-technology line quietly loses hours

The inserter is never the bottleneck — the bench where someone hand-picks taped axial parts is. Here is the invisible cost chain and a five-minute audit that exposes it.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SAF1001 product document and the horizontal taped-feeder operation manual.

Walk the length of a busy smart EMS floor and you will find the bottleneck in the same place in almost every factory: not at the inserter, but beside it, at a small table where an operator is peeling axial components off paper tape with their fingers.

Taped axial parts — resistors, diodes, small inductors, braided jump wires — arrive in packaging that was designed for protection, not for automation. So the line absorbs them the expensive way: seconds per part, by hand, all day. Nobody logs it because the inserter was never the constraint. The constraint is the bench, and the bench is invisible on the capacity spreadsheet.

Here is the five-minute audit. Pick your three highest-volume taped axial parts. For one shift, count how many are hand-picked, time the pick-and-place per part with a phone stopwatch, and multiply by your monthly board volume. Then ask the second question: how many wrong-part or reversed-polarity escapes came from that bench last quarter? The first number prices the labour; the second prices the risk.

Once the bench has a number, the alternative is simple to specify. The SAF1001 locks onto the machine datum with a positioning key and a press block, runs a horizontal taping tray under optical fibre sensing and air-cylinder fine-tuning, and presents taped axial components from 3 × 3 mm up to 6 × 20 mm to the insertion head at ±0.3 mm. The feed cylinder advances the tape, the cut cylinder trims the lead, and the 8-core aviation plug carries the IO handshake. 0.8 seconds per feed replaces a shift of hand-picking.

The compounding part: once axial parts are machine-fed, they enter your normal planning world. Cycle counts become real, changeovers get logged, and the bench's variability leaves your quality conversations. The next product introduction that ships on axial tape stops being a staffing problem — the tray is already running.

ARTICLE 02The 0.8-second question: how fast does your tape path really need to be?

Feeding speed is a promise to the inserter. What 0.8 s per feed actually buys you, and the two failure modes when the tape falls behind.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SAF1001 product document and the horizontal taped-feeder operation manual.

There is a number printed on every axial tape feeder's specification sheet that almost nobody interrogates: the feeding speed. On the SAF1001 it is 0.8 seconds per feed. That single figure is either a promise to your inserter or the reason your line starves.

Think about what the inserter actually asks of the tape path. Every cycle, the head descends, takes a part, and expects the next part to be at the pick position, at the right pitch, in the right attitude, before it returns. If the tape path is slower than the head, the head waits. If the tape path is faster but less accurate, the head mis-picks. Both failures cost the same money — they just wear different masks.

The reusable method is to compare two numbers, not one. Take your inserter's cycle time and your board's axial component count. Multiply: that is the demand side. Now take the feeder's feeding speed — 0.8 s per feed for the SAF1001 — and divide: that is the supply side. If supply is faster than demand, the tape path is never the constraint. If it is slower, you need either a faster feeder or a second lane.

The SAF1001's 0.8 s figure is published in the product document alongside a ±0.3 mm feeding accuracy and an air-pressure speed regulation that lets you tune the advance to the tape. The document also records a 1000-consecutive-feed test and a 48-hour aging test with no abnormalities — the two numbers that tell you the 0.8 s is a sustained rate, not a showroom figure.

Log the speed and the accuracy on your changeover card. The first time a new part family arrives, you will know from the card whether the tape path can keep up before you commit the line.

Send us your inserter's cycle time and your axial count per board. We will tell you honestly whether 0.8 s keeps up, or whether your mix wants a second lane.

"Our parts are special" — every feeder salesperson on earth hears this, and about half the time it is true. The other half is an inventory nobody has measured against a published tape window.

The SAF1001's window is printed in the product document: components from 3 × 3 mm up to 6 × 20 mm, on paper tape wider than 0.2 mm, in three standard widths — 35 mm, 64 mm and 92 mm — with custom widths supported. That sounds narrow until you run your real list against it. Axial resistors: inside. Axial diodes: inside. Small axial inductors and film caps: inside. Braided jump wires: inside. The parts you currently hand-pick are overwhelmingly the parts that fit — they simply arrived on tape that no one automated.

Here is the method: export your component master, filter for package type = axial tape, and sort by annual placements. The top of that list is your automation queue, ranked by the money you already spend on it. The parts below the window — the ones that genuinely do not fit — get their own honest line, and that line is where custom design starts.

For the parts inside the window, the feeder does the rest. The horizontal taping tray accepts the reel, the optical fibre reads the tape index, and the air cylinder fine-tunes the position. For the parts outside it, the documented customisation path adapts tray geometry and fixturing to the component — the same way the SAF1001 itself was designed for the machine datum.

Re-run the export every time the planner adds a part family. The list is a living document, and the top ten rows are a roadmap: they tell you which feeder to buy next, not which one you happen to be missing today.

ARTICLE 04Fibre, air cylinder, ±0.3 mm: the three settings that stop mis-picks

A repeatable tuning method for axial tape feeding — the positioning loop that keeps pitch honest through a full shift.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SAF1001 product document and the horizontal taped-feeder operation manual.

Every axial tape feeder on the floor obeys the same physics, and every mis-pick is one of two sentences: the part stopped moving, or the part moved to the wrong place.

Too little air pressure and the column stalls before the pick zone: the head descends onto an empty tape, the machine errors, someone taps the feeder — the universal gesture of manual intervention — and the cycle time you planned evaporates. Too much and the part overshoots: it rides past the fibre index, sits at the wrong pitch, and the head either misses or picks at an angle. The mis-pick you see is at the head; the cause you missed is three components back.

The method the operation manual encodes is one sensing loop and two cylinders. Sense first: the optical fibre reads the tape index, and the air cylinder fine-tunes the position against it. That loop is what makes ±0.3 mm a real number instead of a wish. Then advance: the feed cylinder pushes the tape, the cut cylinder trims the lead, and both cylinders have independent speed adjustment so the timing can be tuned to the part.

The fibre head is the quiet half of the loop. The manual is explicit: clean it weekly with alcohol. A dusty fibre reads the index late, the positioning loop opens, and the accuracy figure on the spec sheet becomes fiction. One wipe, once a week, is the cheapest maintenance contract you will ever sign.

Log the two cylinder speeds and the four delay settings per part number on the changeover card. The first time a new part family arrives, you will know from the card what to dial before you dial it.

If your parts sit outside the smooth-and-accurate window — too light, too sticky, too long-leaded — tell us what happens at the pick. That is exactly the case the custom design service exists for.

ARTICLE 05U-shaping and lead trimming: what axial feeding actually does to a resistor

The mechanical story of the feed-and-cut cycle, and why the geometry matters more than the speed.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SAF1001 product document and the horizontal taped-feeder operation manual.

An axial tape feeder does two mechanical things well, and both are easy to take for granted until you watch them fail: it advances the tape one pitch at a time, and it trims each lead to a defined length before the head arrives.

Consider what the head actually sees. A taped resistor sits in a paper pocket, leads running straight out of the body. The insertion head wants a U-shape — leads bent down on both sides so the part sits flat on the PCB with the body parallel to the surface. Between the pocket and the pick, the SAF1001's feed cylinder pushes the tape forward, the cut cylinder trims the lead to length, and the forming geometry bends the lead into the U that the head can actually place.

The operation manual documents both cylinders with independent speed adjustment, and the adjustment guide documents the lead-length and pitch adjustment: four screws, two work-pieces, and a repeatable geometry. Loosen screws 1 and 2, move the work-pieces outward, and the lead gets longer; move them inward and it gets shorter. Loosen all four, move both pairs outward, and the pitch gets bigger. That is the whole tuning procedure, and it is in the manual in that order.

This is why the ±0.3 mm accuracy figure matters more than it looks. The head does not pick a component; it picks a position. If the pitch drifts, the U-form drifts with it, and the part that used to sit flat now sits at an angle. The geometry is the promise.

Keep the adjustment guide at the machine and re-verify after any blade or spring change. A new blade cuts at a slightly different height, and the height changes the lead length.

Want the drawings? The stick/tube feeder 3D model and the product document are linked on this page, and our engineers will check them against your machine layout before you order.

ARTICLE 06What 8 kg and 24 volts buys against an operator's shift

The energy maths is a rounding error; the labour maths is the business case. A four-line comparison of machine-fed versus hand-picked axial components.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SAF1001 product document and the horizontal taped-feeder operation manual.

An operator's shift costs a number you pay every month and rarely divide. An eight-kilogram axial tape feeder costs a number you will find on an electricity bill in about four years of rounding.

Put the two side by side. Hand-picking a taped axial component is a reach, a peel, a trim, a place, a check — call it three to eight seconds of skilled attention per part, repeated thousands of times, degrading as the shift wears. The machine version: the tape advances, the lead trims, the head takes it, the cycle counter adds one. The energy cost of that presentation is 24 V at 1 A average — the whole feeder draws less than the monitor on your line supervisor's desk.

This is not a comparison of machines against people; it is a comparison of what each is good at. Hands are brilliant at irregular work and terrible at being a queue. A person who spends a shift peeling axial parts off tape is a quality inspector, a kitter and a problem-solver reduced to a metronome — and the metronome slows down at hour six.

The arithmetic that makes the case concrete takes four inputs: axial components per board, boards per day, your own stopwatch time per hand placement, and your loaded wage. The calculator on this page runs exactly those four lines with your numbers and nothing pre-baked, so you can show it to your CFO without a salesperson in the room.

Then watch the second-order effects over a quarter: the pick errors that used to arrive from the bench, the lane that kept feeding during the changeover, the training conversation that stopped being about dexterity. The watts stay the same; the savings compound.

Run the four lines with your numbers this week. If the answer surprises you, send us the inputs — we will tell you what the same feeder does on your worst part and your best day.

ARTICLE 07The wear parts between you and a stopped line

A published service manual is a maintenance strategy. How naming every cylinder, fibre and blade turns downtime into a two-minute swap.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SAF1001 product document and the horizontal taped-feeder operation manual.

A stopped line is never waiting for a motor. It is waiting for the small mechanical part that took the tape trade for ten thousand cycles — and for someone to know its name.

Open the horizontal taped-feeder operation manual and you find an unusual thing for a device this simple: a named troubleshooting chapter, a parts list, and a wiring table that tells you which signal does what. Feed cylinder, cut cylinder, lifting-height adjust screw, feed claw, optical fibre head, fibre amplifier, solenoid valve, control board, IO board, aviation plug. That list is not paperwork; it is a maintenance strategy printed in advance.

Here is how to use it. Identify the wear items — the parts that live under pressure and motion: the cut blade that trims a thousand leads, the feed claw that pushes the tape, the fibre head that reads the index, the solenoid valve that drives the cylinders. Keep one of each per feeder on the shelf. When a lane misbehaves after the tuning check, you are not diagnosing a mystery; you are swapping a named part in minutes.

The reason this works on an axial tape feeder specifically is the design itself: modular cylinders, a bolt-in control board, a tape path you can see. A feeder whose wear parts are buried inside a sealed assembly gets replaced; a feeder whose wear parts are on a published list gets kept. Keeping is cheaper — and the documented one-day spare parts lead-time means 'cheaper' also means 'today'.

Review the list every time you add a part family to the tray. New geometry, new blade pressures, new wear patterns — the shelf stocking is a living decision, and the named parts make it an easy one.

ARTICLE 08Before you automate axial feeding, run these four numbers

A payback method with your own volumes, your own time study and your own price — plus the three savings the method deliberately leaves out.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the SAF1001 product document and the horizontal taped-feeder operation manual.

Most payback conversations about small automation are dishonest in the same direction: the vendor's spreadsheet finds savings you will never collect. Here is the opposite method — four lines, your numbers, and a bias toward under-claiming.

Line one: what does the bench cost today? Count the axial components per board, the boards per day, and the seconds per hand placement you measured yourself — not the number from a brochure, your number. Line two: what does the feeder actually take over? Be honest: it automates the repeatable picks, not the weird ones. Use the share your process really allows. Line three: your loaded wage and your working days. Line four: divide the quoted feeder price by the annual labour the first three lines freed. If the answer is under twelve months, this is a financial decision, not a capital debate.

The calculator on this page runs those four lines exactly, with nothing pre-baked. No invented time studies, no competitor-bashing multipliers, no price hard-coded anywhere — every money figure is typed in by you.

Now the three savings the method deliberately leaves out, because they are yours to prove: the escapes a manual bench lets through — wrong part, reversed polarity, the component that was pushed in at an angle and failed at reflow; the machine slot a dedicated feeder frees on a crowded bank; and the training cost of the bench itself, which is really the cost of every new hire learning your parts with their fingers.

Every factory that starts measuring axial-fed labour finds it was hiding in someone else's cost line — usually 'consumables' or 'overtime'. The four lines make it visible, and visible is negotiable.

Send us the four numbers. We will turn them into a tray configuration — tape width, spare kit, tuning card — and a quotation that matches the arithmetic you already trust.

13 — FAQ

Answers to the questions this feeder raises

What components can the SAF1001 actually feed?
Taped axial components from 3 × 3 mm up to 6 × 20 mm on 35 / 64 / 92 mm paper tape (custom widths supported): taped resistors, taped triodes and taped jump wires. If your part ships on axial tape today, it is very likely inside the window — send a sample reel and we will confirm the presentation.
Does it fit any machine other than the ones in the video?
The SAF1001 as published uses a positioning key + press block fixing method that supports custom structures. The sister ATF-1002 model in the family is documented on JUKI, Panasonic, Yamaha, FUJI and UIC platforms. Tell us the machine and we quote the interface variant.
How fast can it feed? What throughput should I plan?
The published feeding speed is 0.8 s per feed with air-pressure speed regulation, and feeding accuracy is ±0.3 mm. The tape path presents parts faster than the insertion head can take them — throughput is set by the machine's pick cycle, not the feeder. The product document also records a 1000-consecutive-feed test and a 48-hour aging test with no abnormalities.
What happens when a component jams?
Most jams are tuning, not hardware: air pressure too low (parts stall), fibre head dirty (positioning loop opens), or feed-claw stop position wrong (the claw misses the next part). The operation manual's troubleshooting chapter names each failure mode and the fix. Clean the fibre head weekly with alcohol; check the four cylinder delays after any spring or blade change.
What are the power and utility requirements?
24 V DC at 1 A average / 3 A peak, and 0.4 – 0.6 MPa dry clean compressed air. Both arrive through the 8-core φ16 mm aviation plug and the standard air inlet. The manual is explicit: never short 24 V to 0 V, and never run the inlet below 0.6 MPa or parts will not advance fully.
How does the feeder talk to the inserter?
IO communication through the aviation plug, or standalone operation. The published wiring: host sends a start signal X6, the feeder advances and trims, then sends a ready signal Y3 back; the host clamps the part and returns X7, which releases the cut knife. All signals are 0 V active, switch type.
How long does installation and changeover take?
Mounting is a seat-and-clamp on the machine datum — seconds, with no tools. A tape changeover is dropping a new reel into the tray and recalling the logged delay settings. The full commissioning, including tuning, is a same-shift job.
How do I get a quotation?
Send a photo of your taped components, the tape width, the board volumes and your machine list to info@smthelp.com or WhatsApp +86 13602562576. You get a tray configuration, a spare part kit proposal and a price — usually within one working day, with a sample feeding test available before you commit.
